text:
Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular AppsSwati KhandelwalNov 22, 2026Vulnerability / Application Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.

Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

Updating the Renderer

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable
Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending
SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress

title: SentinelOne Singularity Operations Center - Graph Explorer: Seeing Your Detections as Relationships Instead of Rows
text: Before startsCheck Out old Series > https://www.cyberengage.org/courses-1/mastering-sentinelone%3A-a-comprehensive-guide-to-deep-visibility%2C-threat-hunting%2C-and-advanced-querying%22New Series > https://www.cyberengage.org/courses-1/sentinelonesingularityoperationscenter Every other screen we have covered in this series gives you rows. The alerts list is rows. Deep Visibility is rows. The vulnerability page is rows. Rows are great when you already know what you are looking for.Graph Explorer is the one screen in the Ops Center that does not give you rows. It gives you dots and lines. Every dot is a thing (an endpoint, a user, a cloud resource, an alert, a vulnerability, a misconfiguration) and every line is a relationship between two of those things.So instead of asking "show me the alerts", you ask "show me the machines that have alerts", or "show me the machines that have a critical alert and also a critical vulnerability". That second question is very hard to answer from two separate lists. In the graph it is one query. What it is, and what it is notGraph Explorer is part of the Singularity Graph, and it is only available once the Operations Center is enabled. You will find it in the sidebar as Graph Explorer.The first thing to understand is how it differs from the Storyline, because people mix the two up.Storyline correlates events on one endpoint. Process started, process wrote a file, file made a network connection. It is the story of what happened on that machine.Singularity Graph correlates assets, alerts and exposures across your environment based on how they relate to each other. It is the map of what is connected to what.When you click an alert node in the graph, the alert details open, and from there you can still jump into its Storyline. So the two work together. The graph tells you how wide the problem is. The Storyline tells you what actually happened.The second thing to understand is where the data comes from. The graph supports every asset type that is in the Unified Asset Inventory. That means endpoints, discovered devices, identity assets and cloud assets. But it only knows about what your tenant actually feeds it.If you only run the EDR agent, your graph will mostly be endpoints and the alerts on them. If you also have identity, cloud security or network discovery feeding the inventory, the graph gets much richer, because there are more things to connect. Keep that in mind before you judge the feature on a small tenant. The pieces of the screenThere are four parts to learn.The query builder. This is where you build a query. You pick a starting resource, like Windows desktop or macOS desktop, then click the plus sign to add either a property (a filter on that thing, like Asset status = Active) or a relationship (a link to another thing, like Alerts - has detection of).One rule matters here: a filter applies to the item directly above it, or to the item it is connected to by a line in the builder. So if you add a Severity filter right under an Alerts step, it filters the alerts, not the machines.The builder only offers relationships that make sense for the step you are on. If you are on an endpoint, it will offer alerts, vulnerabilities, networks and so on. You do not need to memorise anything. Click the plus sign and read the menu.The graph itself. The query runs as you build it, and the graph redraws each time. You get the first 20 nodes. If there are more, a Partial results note shows and you click Load more under the graph. The product limits page puts the maximum number of assets returned at 100, so this is not a tool for listing your whole estate. It is a tool for looking at a slice of it.The controls. Along the side of the graph you can switch between graph view and table view, change the layout, open the key that explains each node icon, re-centre, zoom, and export. Pierluigi Paganini

Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents from reading its app on iOS 27 and Android, warning that Gemini and Siri AI threaten its privacy guarantees.

Signal is restricting new AI agents built into iOS 27 and Android from capturing its data, president Meredith Whittaker announced. The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen.

The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you.

This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests.

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.” reads the announcement. “The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant. Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

title: Information and Privacy Commissioner confirms health authority updates following snooping incidents related to Lapu Lapu Day Festival
text:
The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of British Columbia issued a news release:
Following a February 2026 investigation report that revealed 71 snooping incidents by 36 healthcare workers related to the 2025 Lapu Lapu Day Festival, Information and Privacy Commissioner Michael Harvey has confirmed that the health authorities involved (the Fraser Health Authority, the Provincial Health Services Authority, and Vancouver Coastal Health) have addressed the nine recommendations issued in the report.
The investigation report found that the breaches violated section 25.1 of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA), which prohibits unauthorized disclosure of personal information. The Commissioner also found that notification to affected individuals did not occur without unreasonable delay. However, the Commissioner also found that the health authorities have and can build on reasonable safeguards to protect patient data.
The report included nine recommendations to mitigate the breach, strengthen safeguards, and prevent snooping, including:
• Continuing efforts to deploy automated software, with a focus on real-time alert generation and automated access prevention, where possible;
• Reviewing role-based access controls, including efforts to prevent access rights from being inherited or mistakenly applied;
• Notifying affected individuals; and
• Applying disciplinary measures for snooping that are strong enough to effectively sanction and deter snooping, including notifying regulatory colleges as required or appropriate.

title: Cleverbridge warns that hackers stole credit card numbers and CVVs in a data breach. Exposure of both payment details creates a risk of fraudulent transactions. #DataBreach #PaymentSecurity #Cybersecurityhttps://cyberworldops.eu/en/cleverbridge-breach-exposes-card-numbers-and-security-codes
text:
Data Breaches

Illustrative image generated with AI

Customers who paid through Cleverbridge are being warned that attackers stole their payment card details, including the security codes used to verify transactions. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, 2026; a notice reviewed by BleepingComputer for its November 22 report identifies card numbers, expiration dates and CVV/CVC codes as compromised.
The exposure concerns purchases processed through a platform that supports sales, payments and subscriptions for software vendors and software-as-a-service businesses. Cleverbridge names Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony and Parallels among its clients, but has not identified the businesses whose buyers were affected or disclosed the number of affected customers.
Detection and the stolen information
Cleverbridge’s public incident statement, quoted by BleepingComputer, puts detection of unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026. The company temporarily shut systems down as a containment measure and restored them all that same day. Its investigation later established that an outside party had copied payment card data held on the platform.
The public statement directs customers to their individual notices to learn which information was involved. The notification obtained by BleepingComputer provides that detail for one recipient: the number, expiry date and security code of a card used for a Cleverbridge purchase. CVV/CVC codes help verify card transactions, making their inclusion a particular concern.
That notification says the copied information did not include other personal data, giving the recipient’s name, contact information and billing details as examples. It identifies the compromised card through its final four digits, which BleepingComputer concealed in its report.
Cleverbridge says the breach involved neither ransomware nor encryption of its systems by the attackers. How the intruders entered and how long they had access remain undisclosed. BleepingComputer sought answers about the entry method, customer count, whether the stolen card information was encrypted and why the security codes were accessible; the company had not replied by publication.
Guidance for affected cardholders
Cleverbridge says it has alerted law enforcement and data protection authorities, along with payment card networks and payment partners. It has also engaged TransUnion’s Cyberscout to help deliver notifications and offer affected customers free credit monitoring and fraud assistance.
For customers receiving a breach notice, Cleverbridge recommends checking payment card statements for transactions they did not authorize. It also advises contacting the card issuer about the exposure, since the bank may decide to replace the compromised card.

Security

A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

Zack Whittaker

7:46 AM PST · November 20, 2026

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

“Basic human error”

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Threat Wrap
Tower Records Has a New Distribution Model

TP

The Perimeter Desk
Threat Wrap

2026-11-22

# Tower Records Has a New Distribution Model

The most surprising number on the wire this midday is 10.2 million. That is the number of accounts compromised in the recent breach at Tower Records Japan. It's an odd feeling to see a record store topping the volume charts for data theft, but it highlights a persistent habit in retail: collecting more identity data than is required to sell a plastic disc or a piece of vinyl. When a company holds ten million records for a niche hobbyist market, they aren't just running a shop; they're running a high-value target for anyone looking to build credential-stuffing lists.

Then there's the situation in South Korea. KEPCO—the Korea Electric Power Corporation—has confirmed another breach affecting just over 1.5 million people. This isn't just a leak of email addresses. We're talking about resident registration numbers and bank account details. In South Korea, the resident registration number is the primary key for almost every civic interaction. Once that’s out, you aren't just worried about phishing; you're worried about total identity replacement.

It’s a stark reminder that energy and utilities are currently the ninth most targeted sector this week, with ten new incidents reported today alone. The danger here isn't just data theft. If an attacker can pivot from the billing database to the operational technology (OT) side of a power grid, you move from "stolen identities" to "dark cities."

The real institutional disaster, however, is the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC) breach. The government sector remains the primary target for attackers this week, with 363 stories logged over the last seven days and 51 new entries today. The NCIC is effectively the central nervous system for American law enforcement; it's where cops check if a car is stolen or if a suspect has active warrants.

Whenever these breaches happen, some executive will likely describe their security as "military-grade." I hate that phrase. It’s marketing shorthand for "we bought an expensive box and hoped it worked." In reality, the NCIC breach isn't a failure of encryption; it's almost certainly a failure of access control.

The second-order effect here is the one nobody is talking about: street-level trust. If a police officer pulls over a vehicle and the NCIC returns "clean" because an attacker has been scrubbing records, or if the data is simply untrustworthy, the safety of every officer on the road drops. When the integrity of the primary truth-source for law enforcement vanishes, you don't just have a data breach; you have a systemic failure of public safety.

While we’re talking about institutional failures, let's look at the Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw that’s been exploited to access tenant data. This is where I want to get technical, because this isn't a "crypto flaw." It's a key-management and permissioning disaster.

To understand what happened, you have to understand how identity synchronization works between an on-premises environment and the cloud. Entra Connect Health acts as a bridge. In a healthy setup, the bridge should only carry specific telemetry about the health of the sync process. However, the flaw here allowed attackers to move from that "health" reporting channel into actual tenant data.

Think of it like this: you give a contractor a key to your utility closet so they can check the water heater (the health check). But because of a flaw in how the locks were installed, that same key unexpectedly opens the vault where you keep the deeds to the house (the tenant data).

Claude Shannon, the father of information theory, spent a lot of time thinking about entropy and the unpredictability of messages. text:
Following inference data

Why does AI inference data matter?

How do AI routers expose your prompts?

Three compromised companies

Marketplace resellers stole customer prompts

Privacy settings and retention policies were ignored

How do canary tokens detect prompt leaks?

What we did about it

How can you protect your AI supply chain?

HD Moore, Chief Research Officer, will be regularly sharing work from the research team he leads at Dragos. Topics will include xOT, IT, LLMs, PQC, and more. Their findings will sharpen defenders’ understanding of exposures and vulnerabilities emerging across the threat landscape.We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced. What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.Over a five-month period from July through November 2026, we submitted approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to widely used AI services and monitored what happened after inference. Our investigation uncovered three significant findings:Evidence of provider compromises. We observed activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed. Our seeded test prompts were used in attempts to access our controlled test systems and canary AWS accounts.Unauthorized access to customer prompts by inference marketplace providers. Multiple resellers operating through an AI inference marketplace were able to view and retain customer prompts using standard logging capabilities, without exploiting a vulnerability or bypassing platform controls.Failures in privacy and data-handling practices. We observed multiple cases in which providers appeared not to honor customer privacy settings or published policies. Examples included prompts submitted to U.S.-based providers being transmitted to Chinese AI organizations, unique URLs being accessed months after a single inference request, and one seeded link ultimately appearing in an internal company chat in China.
Following inference data

We wanted to understand what happens to inference data after it leaves the customer’s environment.To answer that question, we created millions of unique canaries, including URLs and credentials that would never be used by legitimate systems. Any attempt to access those assets would indicate that someone, somewhere in the AI ecosystem had seen the original prompt.The results exposed a fundamental disconnect between how AI services are marketed and how inference data is handled in practice.
Why does AI inference data matter?

Most folks picture AI inference as a question and a response. Text goes in, GPUs juggle some bits, and text comes back out. What complicates this is how the data is actually treated. AI providers commonly store prompts and responses for operational, training, safety, abuse-monitoring, or business purposes. Depending on the provider, that data may be retained for days, months, or indefinitely. It may also traverse multiple organizations, including model developers, cloud operators, inference platforms, and third-party resellers.The prompts and replies – the inference data itself – are often more valuable than the GPU resources used to process them. They frequently contain confidential source code, internal communications, strategic plans, customer information, credentials, and other sensitive business data.
How do AI routers expose your prompts?

AI routers work by offering a single API endpoint that forwards your request to a pool of available models, sometimes at different hosting providers, with unified billing. Routers are great at cost reduction and providing flexibility without managing multiple accounts and credentials. The path to the inference server often passes through more than one router before reaching another provider, and from there the specific server hosting the target model. title: Revealed: profiles of UK experts on gambling harm being hijacked to push illegal online casinos
text: At least six prominent academics seem to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenAt least six prominent academics seem to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy Revealed: profiles of UK experts on gambling harm being hijacked to push illegal online casinosFindings highlight unscrupulous tactics used by operators in multibillion pound illicit market and challenges facing authorities Prof Heather Wardle has dedicated 20 years to researching the harm caused by gambling.So the University of Glasgow social scientist was horrified to learn that her reputation and even her photograph had been hijacked by rogue casinos claiming her endorsement for the very games whose addictive properties she has documented.“I would never review these things and promote them to people,” she said. “It’s completely out of kilter with the research I’ve conducted across my entire career.”Wardle is far from alone in being targeted like this, evidence reviewed by the Guardian suggests.At least six prominent academics appear to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Most appear to be “affiliates”, businesses that earn commission by directing online traffic towards gambling firms. Several of the websites promoted unlicensed casinos that are not on GamStop, a UK scheme to help people suffering from problem gambling shut themselves out of betting sites.Nor is it just academics whose public profile appears to have been misused in this way. Dozens of websites with no previous links to betting appear to have been bought up on the cheap and redesigned, capitalising on their existing search engine recognition.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a deliberate misuse of our profiles to mislead consumers into believing that these products are safe,’ Prof Heather Wardle said. Photograph: University of GlasgowThe result is that people visiting what they think is a site dedicated to politics, tourism or even HIV research, can end up being lured in by offshore casinos.The findings highlight not just the unscrupulous tactics used by the multibillion-pound illicit market but also the enormous challenge facing the UK authorities.‘It’s completely egregious’One site, called 666 Casino, features a photo of a smiling Wardle, described as “the woman behind the reviews”.“Every trustworthy casino review needs someone who’s actually done the legwork, and that’s precisely the role Heather Wardle has carved out for herself in the UK gambling content space,” it reads.In a lengthy “biography”, the page claims she began as a casual online gambler but later began analysing and rating the best casinos, including the quality of their bonuses and the speed of cash withdrawals.“I was saddened but I wasn’t surprised,” said Wardle. “Some quarters of the gambling industry will go far to undermine academics who are doing work in the public interest.”Wardle is one of at least six prominent academics whose reputations, built on their research into how gambling can exploit and harm people, have been co-opted in this way. RIKEN, a prominent Japanese scientific research institution, confirmed a cyberattack on November 13, 2026, that forced the Fugaku supercomputer offline. Investigators found that an unknown party used an online operational status dashboard as a stepping stone to enter the internal network between November 10 and November 13. The institution stopped all running and waiting computational jobs to prevent the attackers from running unauthorized workloads.The potentially exposed data includes:Full names, email addresses, and user IDsSSH private keys and access keys for external servicesResearch data stored in user home directoriesThe incident affected 4,222 registered users of Fugaku and 375 users of the Rikyu system. RIKEN reported that attackers attempted to use stolen credentials to connect to other external systems. The organization is currently working with operators of other supercomputing facilities to check for secondary intrusions. Research files were accessible, but RIKEN has not confirmed if any specific datasets were stolen.RIKEN notified the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology. The institution isolated the compromised dashboard, replaced management keys, and disabled all user public keys. RIKEN plans to rebuild the affected servers and implement AI-based security monitoring before resuming operations. Users are advised to revoke any credentials that were stored on Fugaku and be careful of phishing attempts using the RIKEN name.

It's 3 a.m. The call comes in because someone finally admitted that the National Crime Information Center database is compromised; if you don't know what NCIC stands for, it is the central nervous system for American law enforcement. It isn't just another server rattling around in a basement. When this goes down, we aren't talking about leaked emails or some mid-level admin's forgotten password, and this hits at the very integrity of criminal justice data across the entire country.

Right now, Government sits squarely at number one on the targeting list. I have seen 374 stories just this week, and today alone added another 56 to that pile. The volume is staggering, sure. But usually, high volume is just noise. This? This isn't noise.

The NCIC breach is clearly the lead story, but it doesn't live in a vacuum. Consider what else happened. The USDA took some portals offline this week after dealing with a cybersecurity incident. Meanwhile, Russian espionage operations have been intercepting emails from officials at both NATO and the EU. Look closer: all three are hits on the Government sector, and one looks like administrative failure, one is probably a clumsy breach, and one is high-tier statecraft.

The pattern here isn't a single exploit. It reflects a systemic willingness to target the machinery of the state during this period of extreme leadership churn; the White House named a new cybersecurity chief just hours after the previous one quit. That kind of vacuum at the top usually filters down as hesitation in the SOC and confusion in policy. Attackers don't care about our org chart, but they notice when nobody is steering the ship.

Defenders in this sector are fighting on two fronts simultaneously, and on one side are the noisy attackers hitting USDA portals and causing outages that make the news. On the other side you have silent operators intercepting NATO traffic. The danger isn't the outage; it's the silence, and if you're an analyst in a government SOC right now, your biggest fear isn't a system going down. It is the fact that everything looks normal while a foreign intelligence service reads your diplomatic cables in real time.

The common argument from the policy side is that these are isolated incidents, and they will tell you the USDA outage is unrelated to the NCIC breach, and that neither has anything to do with NATO emails. They want to categorize these as "legacy debt" or "unfortunate coincidences."

That's a loser's argument.

This isn't some random fluke, and when you see law enforcement, agriculture, and international diplomacy getting hit at once, it's a plan. They are mapping out how the state machinery works. The attackers stopped looking for one big prize because they figured out the government is just a bunch of linked prizes with different security levels.

The ripple effects are the worst part. Look at the NCIC breach. That's not just an FBI headache. Every local cop and sheriff who uses that database for live intelligence now has a trust problem. # Who's Actually Behind the Supplier Wave?

A ghost is running the show this week. Look at the data and you'll see the biggest threat isn't some gang with a brand or a manifesto. They're just "unknown cybercriminals. These people showed up in 16 stories over seven days; the industry uses that label when attackers don't brag on leak sites or leave ransom notes. They just take what they want and go.

It's jarring. Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) says 1.52 million records were stolen, and that includes account numbers and resident registrations. Why are so many credit unions getting hit at the same time? One supplier got breached. Then you have the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database, and an apparent hack left it a mess and has the FBI scrambling.

When you see this pattern, you aren't looking at a surgical strike. You're looking at a harvest.

The playbook here isn't about "hacking" in the cinematic sense. It's about finding one weak link in a supply chain and using it to pivot into a hundred different targets. The exploitation of a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a prime example of this. These attackers find a technical hole that allows them to move across tenants, and then they just keep sliding until they hit something valuable.

The attribution for these hits is mostly wishful thinking right now. Some are calling it state-sponsored espionage; others say it's just high-end criminals looking for a payday. In my experience, the distinction doesn't matter to a business with ten employees and no dedicated security person. Whether the attacker is a government operative or a guy in a basement, the result is the same: your data is on a forum and your systems are locked.

The real danger here isn't the initial breach, but the second-order effect. When a supplier for dozens of credit unions gets hit, it isn't just those banks that suffer. Every customer of those banks now has their personal info floating around. That leads to a surge in highly targeted phishing attacks against individuals who have no idea why they are being targeted. If you run a small professional services firm, your clients—who might be these same bank customers—are suddenly much more vulnerable to social engineering.

Some people will argue that a ten-person shop is too small to be a target for this kind of operation. They'll say the attackers want KEPCO, not a local accounting office.

That's a dangerous misunderstanding of how modern attacks work. You aren't the target; you're the path. Attackers love small firms because they often have trusted relationships with larger targets but lack the budget for a full-time security lead. If an attacker can compromise your email, they can send a "perfect" invoice or a "urgent" document to your biggest client, and it will be trusted because it came from you.

An enterprise handles this by spending north of six figures on managed detection and response (MDR) and an army of analysts staring at dashboards. You can't do that. You have to rely on boring controls.

I distrust any consultant who tells you to "simply deploy" a complex AI-driven security stack. For a small shop, the only things that actually move the needle are the basics we all ignore because they're tedious.

A foreign currency exchange shop in Chiang Mai looked like an ordinary money changer. Thai police now say it was a laundromat for scam cash, with Tether’s USDT as the detergent.
Thailand’s Cyber Crime Investigation Bureau disclosed on November 20, 2026 that it had dismantled the operation. Police say a wallet linked to the main suspect recorded a turnover of more than 2.7 million USDT, valued at roughly 92 million baht.

The man allegedly behind it all was not there to see the raids. He had already left the country.
How the alleged scheme worked
According to investigators, the shop served as a front for converting proceeds from online investment scams into USDT stablecoins. The scams in question were mainly fake share schemes pushed through social media.
The flow of money, as police describe it, ran in stages. Victims sent funds into a network of 24 mule bank accounts, which then moved the cash toward brokers for conversion.
Once the money reached the shop, it was allegedly swapped into USDT. The operators reportedly took a commission of 2-3% for the service.
Four victims have so far reported losses totaling 9,435,607.97 baht, which works out to about $275,000 to $280,000. That figure covers only the people who have come forward.

The wallet data tells a much bigger story. Police said the suspect’s digital wallet logged a turnover of over 2,749,566 USDT, worth about 92 million baht.
Meanwhile, the exchange shop’s official books looked rather sleepy. It declared revenue of just 443,025 baht over nine months.

Who was arrested, and who got away
Police carried out the raids on November 10, 2026. They hit the currency exchange shop and a residence in Doi Saket, a district in Chiang Mai province.
The main suspect is Wenjun Feng, a 42-year-old Chinese national. He fled Thailand before officers arrived.
An arrest warrant for Feng had been issued months earlier. He is now on an immigration watchlist.
Two people were detained. The first is Feng’s wife, 36-year-old Yaning Yan, who faces charges under Thailand’s Foreign Business Act.
The second is Juthamas Meechai, a 35-year-old Thai national. She served as the shop’s director and majority owner, and she has been charged with nominee and false-statement offenses.
Why USDT keeps showing up in these cases
The research behind the case points to a wider pattern. Transnational scam networks involving Chinese operators have been exploiting unlicensed exchanges in Thailand to launder money through digital assets.
USDT sits at the center of that pattern. Its appeal to launderers comes down to two things: deep liquidity and fast transfers that move faster than traditional banking channels.
There is an irony here worth noting. The same blockchain that makes USDT fast also makes it traceable, which is how police were able to put a figure on the wallet’s turnover in the first place.
What this means for Thailand’s crypto market
The investigation itself is not finished. Police say the case may expand to identify additional victims and more linked financial accounts.
That matters because the numbers do not yet line up neatly. Four reported victims account for under 10 million baht, while the wallet allegedly processed around 92 million baht worth of USDT.
The other open thread is Feng himself. With the alleged mastermind abroad and an arrest warrant pending, the people facing charges right now are the ones who stayed behind.

Sworn in as DOW’s CIO in December 2025, Davies will replace Sean Cairncross, who was confirmed as the top cybersecurity official in August 2025, more than five months after being nominated for the position.

Before her DOW tenure, Davies led cybersecurity at multiple organizations. She served as CISO at Unilever, The Estée Lauder Companies Inc., Hewlett-Packard, and Siemens, and as CSO at Barclays, and founded and was the CEO of the Institute for Cyber.

“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Threema audit unveils Android biometric lock flaw, fix due in December
November 21, 2026 By Bill Mann — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebook

An independent security audit of Threema’s Android and iOS apps found one weakness in the Android biometric app lock but no critical vulnerabilities.

Threema says the fix is scheduled for December in Android version 6.7.0.

Assured Security Consultants’ Jimmie Rudvall and Wictor Olsson spent 18 person-days reviewing the Android and iOS editions of Threema Private and Threema Work between September 14 and October 2, 2026. They used OWASP’s Mobile Application Security Verification Standard as a baseline, combining automated scans, runtime testing, and manual code review. The auditors manually verified every finding surfaced with help from a large language model.

Threema is a Swiss messaging service that offers end-to-end encryption for messages, calls, and media. Threema Private is its consumer app, while Threema Work is aimed at businesses and public-sector organizations.

How the biometric lock works

Assured found that Threema’s Android app lock relies on a success signal from the operating system’s biometric prompt. In a modified environment, an attacker who could manipulate how the app runs might be able to unlock it without a valid biometric check. Assured rated the risk as low and recommended tying successful biometric verification to a cryptographic operation backed by the Android Keystore.

The auditors rated the apps’ storage and cryptography controls highly. They highlighted Android’s use of SQLCipher to encrypt local data and iOS’s use of the Keychain to protect cryptographic keys and identity credentials. They also noted privacy controls that hide sensitive content in notifications and widgets.

Threema keeps its file encryption design

One of the audit’s three informational findings concerned how Threema encrypts uploaded files and photos. The app uses fixed values known as nonces alongside a fresh random 256-bit key for each encryption operation.

Assured said the fresh keys prevent the usual nonce-reuse problem in normal operation and recommended randomizing the nonce as an extra safeguard. Threema says the change would reduce efficiency and break backward compatibility. It will revisit the decision if it redesigns its cryptography.

Assured marked the other two notes as resolved. One concerned known flaws in Rust dependencies that Threema said were used only in a test tool and excluded from production builds. The other concerned a potential script injection issue in an iOS settings screen. Assured found no way for an attacker to supply input to the affected code in the shipped app and verified that Threema rewrote it to remove the unsafe pattern.

Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed

Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad.

Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage, and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers.

According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately.

“”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage.” Reuters reports.

The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately.

An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad.

“An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added.

The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used.

The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF, the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks.

“The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF. “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks.
